title: India Eyes Entry Into GCAP Fighter Jet Program as Consortium Sets Deadline for New Partners
excerpt: Leonardo CEO Lorenzo Mariani says new countries must commit within a year as India confirms interest in joining the UK-Japan-Italy sixth-generation stealth fighter project.
body:
• Leonardo CEO Lorenzo Mariani said at the Farnborough Airshow that any new country wanting to join GCAP must decide by mid-2027 at the latest, given the program's 2035 flight target.
  • India confirmed in March 2026 that it is evaluating participation in either GCAP or the rival Franco-German-Spanish FCAS program to fill a growing fighter squadron gap.
  • Canada became GCAP's first observer nation on July 21, while Germany is also being considered after the Franco-German SCAF program collapsed in June.
  • Japan approached India in February 2025 about joining, though concerns persist over technology transfer risks tied to India's defense relationship with Russia.

The Clock Is Ticking

The consortium behind the world's most ambitious fighter jet program has given prospective partners a firm deadline. Lorenzo Mariani, CEO of Italian defense giant Leonardo, told Reuters at the Farnborough Airshow on July 22 that any country looking to join the Global Combat Air Programme must commit by the end of 2026 — or at the very latest, within 12 months.

"My personal opinion, 2026 — maximum one year from now," Mariani said, stressing that the 2035 target for the aircraft to be operational leaves little room for negotiation.

GCAP, a joint venture between the United Kingdom, Italy, and Japan, aims to produce a sixth-generation stealth fighter as a successor to the Eurofighter Typhoon and Japan's F-2. The program is being developed through Edgewing, a joint company equally owned by BAE Systems, Leonardo, and Japan Aircraft Industrial Enhancement, with an estimated development cost of $32.5 billion.

India's Fighter Gap

India is among the most closely watched potential entrants. On March 18, India's Chief of Defence Staff General Anil Chauhan confirmed to a Parliamentary Standing Committee that the Indian Air Force is actively evaluating participation in one of two European sixth-generation fighter consortia — GCAP or the Future Combat Air System led by France, Germany, and Spain.

The urgency is clear. The IAF currently operates roughly 29 fighter squadrons against an authorized strength of 42, a gap that has widened as aging MiG-21s are retired and deliveries of the domestically built Tejas Mk1A face delays. India's own fifth-generation program, the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft, remains years from operational readiness.

"There has been no formal decision, but the interest is genuine. India needs access to sixth-generation technology that its indigenous programs cannot deliver in the required timeframe."

— Senior Indian defense official, according to Army Recognition

Japan's Overture — and Its Limits

Japan took the first concrete step toward bringing India into the fold. According to Kyodo News, Japanese government representatives visited New Delhi in February 2025 to brief Indian officials on GCAP and formally invite India to participate. The move was driven by Japan's desire to share the program's rising costs and deepen Indo-Pacific defense ties.

India's Modi government reportedly showed interest, viewing the proposal as compatible with its "Make in India" defense manufacturing push. But the invitation has not been without friction. Japanese defense officials have privately raised concerns about India's operational use of Russia's S-400 air defense system, worried that sharing advanced GCAP technology could create pathways for leaks to Moscow.

"Are we sure we won't just have our technology extracted?" one Japanese defense ministry source told Kyodo, capturing the unease within Tokyo's defense establishment.

A Widening Field

India is not the only country in the queue. Canada signed on as GCAP's first observer nation on July 21, a move that came at the Farnborough Airshow and was seen as a signal of Ottawa's growing willingness to diversify its defense procurement away from the United States amid ongoing trade tensions with Washington.

Germany has emerged as another serious contender. The rival Franco-German SCAF fighter program effectively collapsed in June after years of disputes between Paris and Berlin over workshare and technology rights. With a growing defense budget and existing collaboration on the Eurofighter Typhoon, Germany is considered a natural fit — though some GCAP executives have warned that adding partners risks delaying the program.

Mariani acknowledged continued Saudi interest as well. "I think, I believe, there is still an interest of Saudi to be part of this programme," he said. Japan has historically opposed Saudi participation over concerns about export controls and program timelines.

What's Next

The UK's new government under Prime Minister Andy Burnham has signaled strong support for GCAP. In early July, the consortium awarded a £4.6 billion contract to advance development, and Mariani suggested the 2035 timeline could even be accelerated.

For India, the calculation is complex. Joining GCAP would give the IAF access to technologies — including stealth design, AI-enabled operations, and manned-unmanned teaming — that its indigenous AMCA program is unlikely to deliver before the late 2030s. But it would also require navigating sensitivities around its Russia relationship and potentially accepting limits on how it uses and transfers the technology it acquires.

The Parliamentary committee's recommendation was unambiguous: evaluate and engage. Whether New Delhi moves from evaluation to commitment before Mariani's deadline expires will be one of the most consequential defense decisions India makes this decade.
nri_angle: India's potential entry into GCAP could reshape defense procurement partnerships and offer Indian defense manufacturers opportunities in a multinational program alongside the UK, Japan, and Italy.
